info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 12.3: AI-Assisted Commentary Drafting, Intertextual Verification, and Philological Vetting.

name.text: 01 Question: Entering Step 3: AI-Assisted Commentary Drafting

questiontext.text: Why must human editors audit commentary notes drafted by generative AI models?

generalfeedback.text: AI models generate commentary quickly through semantic inference, but human editors must verify every claim against primary sources.

answer.text: Because AI models predict words based on statistical patterns and can fabricate citations unless checked against primary sources.

feedback.text: Correct. Language models predict plausible text but do not inherently know whether historical claims or citations are true.

answer.text: Because AI models cannot generate English sentences grammatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern AI models write fluent, highly grammatical prose; the danger is factual inaccuracy.

answer.text: Because the TEI guidelines strictly forbid computers from drafting XML.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI markup supports recording computational provenance through the @resp attribute.

answer.text: Because AI models run too slowly to produce useful drafts in a classroom.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Generative models produce drafts in seconds; speed is their main advantage.

name.text: 02 Question: Semantic Inference vs Lexical Matching

questiontext.text: How does AI semantic inference differ from rule-based lexical matching when analyzing historical texts?

generalfeedback.text: Semantic inference allows AI models to connect related ideas across different vocabularies, acting as powerful hypothesis generators.

answer.text: Semantic inference recognizes related concepts, synonyms, and themes even when no exact words are shared.

feedback.text: Correct. By modeling words in high-dimensional vector spaces, AI connects thematic ideas across differing vocabularies.

answer.text: Semantic inference only works on numbers and dates, while lexical matching works on letters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both techniques analyze textual words and phrases.

answer.text: Semantic inference guarantees 100% historical truth with zero errors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Semantic inference is prone to hallucinating connections that never existed.

answer.text: Lexical matching understands poetic metaphors better than neural networks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Lexical matching is blind to metaphors unless words match character-for-character.

name.text: 03 Question: AI Capabilities in Commentary Drafting

questiontext.text: Which editorial task is an AI assistant best suited to perform when drafting commentary?

generalfeedback.text: AI models speed up commentary drafting by providing historical summaries, defining specialized terms, and structuring note metadata.

answer.text: Summarizing broad historical context, explaining archaic terms, and structuring prose notes into XML templates.

feedback.text: Correct. AI models excel at rapid contextual summarization, term definition, and data formatting.

answer.text: Conducting physical chemical tests on the paper fibers of the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI software has no physical sensors to test paper fibers.

answer.text: Guaranteeing that archival documents in local libraries will never suffer fire damage.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital software cannot provide physical disaster protection.

answer.text: Replacing human historians on academic editorial boards.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI is an editorial assistant, not a replacement for human scholarship.

name.text: 04 Question: The Epistemic Hazard: Citation Hallucination

questiontext.text: What is citation hallucination in generative AI commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Because AI models predict words statistically, they can fabricate citations and historical evidence that appear completely genuine.

answer.text: The fabrication of non-existent primary sources, book titles, archive references, or volume numbers that appear genuine.

feedback.text: Correct. Because models predict plausible-sounding words, they frequently invent realistic citations that do not exist.

answer.text: A technical glitch that deletes the user's hard drive during an AI query.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hallucination refers to generating false textual information, not disk formatting.

answer.text: When an AI model translates French text into Italian instead of English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language confusion is a translation error, not citation fabrication.

answer.text: When a scanner misreads a letter due to low optical resolution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Optical character misrecognition is an OCR scanning error.

name.text: 05 Question: Cohort Hallucination Audit: Treaty Clauses and Maud Lewis

questiontext.text: Why did the AI model hallucinate an 'Article 9' when prompted about Andromeda's 1752 Peace and Friendship Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Never accept AI claims about archival people or legal articles without checking the primary documents directly.

answer.text: Because the model blended patterns from other colonial records, failing to recognize that the 1752 treaty contains only eight articles.

feedback.text: Correct. The model generated plausible colonial legal language without checking the primary document's eight-article boundary.

answer.text: Because the 1752 Treaty was written in modern French.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The 1752 Halifax treaty was composed in English.

answer.text: Because the Nova Scotia Archives removed Article 9 in 2020.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The historical 1752 manuscript has always consisted of eight articles.

answer.text: Because AI models refuse to read treaties written before 1800.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models process texts from all historical eras.

name.text: 06 Question: Historical Anachronism and Conceptual Flattening

questiontext.text: What is 'conceptual flattening' in AI-generated historical commentary?

generalfeedback.text: AI models tend to project modern ideas onto historical records, requiring editors to guard against anachronism.

answer.text: Erasing unique historical differences by explaining past ideas through familiar modern categories.

feedback.text: Correct. Conceptual flattening strips away the distinctive historical peculiarities of 18th-century practices.

answer.text: Compressing an image file into a low-resolution JPEG.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Conceptual flattening is an intellectual distortion of historical ideas, not image compression.

answer.text: Ironing a wrinkled parchment page before photography.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Physical conservation is unrelated to conceptual flattening.

answer.text: Converting all fonts in a TEI file to Arial.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Font styling is a layout choice, not conceptual flattening.

name.text: 07 Question: Automation Bias and Editorial Vigilance

questiontext.text: How can an editor counter automation bias when reviewing AI commentary drafts in VS Code?

generalfeedback.text: Automation bias leads scholars to trust fluent AI prose; editors must actively verify dates, names, and quotes against primary files.

answer.text: By actively verifying every date, person, and quoted string against primary files in the workspace.

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial vigilance requires checking every factual claim rather than trusting fluent prose uncritically.

answer.text: By accepting all suggestions without reading them to finish the assignment faster.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Uncritical acceptance is the exact definition of automation bias.

answer.text: By turning off the computer monitor and guessing the answers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Guessing blindly does not produce scholarly work.

answer.text: By deleting the primary transcription file completely.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Primary transcription files are the foundation of your digital edition.

name.text: 08 Question: The Epistemic Boundary: Public History vs Archival Witnesses

questiontext.text: What falls outside an AI model's epistemic boundary when analyzing unique archival manuscripts?

generalfeedback.text: AI models excel at general historical background but know nothing about the physical peculiarities of your unique archival manuscript.

answer.text: The physical ink strokes, unique margin notes, and specific archival corrections on your particular manuscript copy.

feedback.text: Correct. While models know broad historical facts, they have never inspected the physical peculiarities of your unique witness.

answer.text: The year the French Revolution began.

feedback.text: Incorrect. General public dates fall squarely within the AI model's training data.

answer.text: The names of famous British monarchs like King George II.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Broad historical figures are well known to AI models.

answer.text: The general definition of paper currency in economic history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Broad conceptual history is easily handled by AI models.

name.text: 09 Question: Designing Structured System Prompts for Commentary

questiontext.text: What is the primary benefit of including the target span's xml:id in a commentary system prompt?

generalfeedback.text: Structured system prompts define roles, context, target spans, and categories, forcing the AI to generate disciplined commentary drafts.

answer.text: It anchors the model's attention to an exact passage and ensures the output note links to a stable XML identifier.

feedback.text: Correct. Providing the specific xml:id tethers the generated note directly to your transcription markup.

answer.text: It automatically purchases a software license for the AI model.

feedback.text: Incorrect. An xml:id is a markup identifier, not a financial payment token.

answer.text: It prevents anyone on the internet from reading your commentary.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML IDs organize internal document structure, not internet firewalls.

answer.text: It forces the model to write in Latin instead of English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language output is governed by role instructions, not XML ID tags.

name.text: 10 Question: Negative Prompt Constraints and Guardrails

questiontext.text: Why is instructing an AI model to output '[UNVERIFIED]' for uncertain claims an effective guardrail?

generalfeedback.text: Negative prompt constraints prevent hallucinations by explicitly forbidding invented citations and demanding [UNVERIFIED] flags for uncertain claims.

answer.text: It permits the model to admit ignorance rather than inventing a plausible lie or hallucinated citation.

feedback.text: Correct. Demanding an explicit flag for uncertainty breaks the model's tendency to fabricate facts.

answer.text: Because [UNVERIFIED] causes VS Code to shut down automatically.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VS Code treats [UNVERIFIED] as ordinary text.

answer.text: Because the TEI validator crashes if it encounters uncertainty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI markup supports editorial uncertainty through elements like and .

answer.text: Because it proves that the student did not do any homework.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Identifying unverified claims is an essential step in honest research.

name.text: 11 Question: Schema-Constrained Generation: Structured JSON and TEI Output

questiontext.text: Why is requesting JSON or XML output better than requesting free-flowing paragraphs for digital commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Requesting JSON or XML output forces the model to structure its commentary notes into distinct, machine-readable fields.

answer.text: It forces the model to separate targets, categories, claims, and citations into machine-readable fields that scripts can parse.

feedback.text: Correct. Schema-constrained outputs allow automated validation and seamless integration into digital editions.

answer.text: Because JSON files take up zero bytes of storage space on disk.

feedback.text: Incorrect. JSON files occupy memory like any text file.

answer.text: Because free-flowing paragraphs are illegal under copyright law.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Prose paragraphs are completely legal but harder to parse computationally.

answer.text: Because XML cannot be read by human beings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML is designed to be readable by both humans and machines.

name.text: 12 Question: Anchoring AI Notes to Stable XML Identifiers

questiontext.text: In TEI standoff commentary, what is the role of the @resp attribute on an AI-generated note?

generalfeedback.text: AI-drafted commentary notes must point to valid xml:id anchors in your transcription, with provenance tracked in the resp attribute.

answer.text: It transparently attributes the note's drafting origin to an AI assistant rather than human scholarship.

feedback.text: Correct. The @resp attribute tracks editorial provenance, distinguishing machine drafts from human vetting.

answer.text: It specifies how many seconds the AI took to draft the sentence.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The @resp attribute indicates responsibility, not execution runtime.

answer.text: It changes the background color of the webpage to red.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance attributes carry editorial metadata, not visual styling.

answer.text: It prevents other scholars from citing the note.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Stating machine provenance informs readers without preventing citation.

name.text: 13 Question: Philological Vetting: 18th-Century French and Colonial English

questiontext.text: Why did the unvetted AI model incorrectly define 'Truckhouse' as an automobile repair garage in the 1752 Treaty?

generalfeedback.text: Philological vetting catches humorous or misleading modern readings of historical vocabulary, restoring true archival meaning.

answer.text: Because the model applied a modern 20th-century definition instead of the historical 18th-century meaning of a regulated fur-trading post.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical vetting catches anachronistic vocabulary shifts and restores authentic archival meaning.

answer.text: Because the British army used pickup trucks during the Seven Years' War.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Motor vehicles were invented over a century after the 1752 treaty.

answer.text: Because the treaty was translated into German before reaching Halifax.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The treaty was negotiated in English and Mi'kmaq.

answer.text: Because the scribe wrote 'garage' in the margins of the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The word garage does not appear in 18th-century colonial treaty manuscripts.

name.text: 14 Question: Intertextual Allusion Detection: Real vs Imagined Parallels

questiontext.text: How should an editor verify an AI model's claim that a document quotes an earlier historical work?

generalfeedback.text: AI models discover interesting thematic parallels, but editors must verify whether an echo represents genuine historical borrowing or coincidence.

answer.text: By confirming that both texts share distinctive verbatim phrasing or documented historical borrowing, rather than mere thematic coincidence.

feedback.text: Correct. Editors must distinguish deliberate borrowing from general cultural or topical overlap.

answer.text: By accepting the claim if the AI sounds confident and polite.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI confidence has no correlation with historical accuracy.

answer.text: By deleting both documents from the course syllabus.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editors analyze documents rather than deleting them.

answer.text: By checking if both texts were printed in the exact same year.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Borrowing occurs across different years; identical printing dates do not prove intertextuality.

name.text: 15 Question: Entity Linking and Authority Control (Wikidata and VIAF)

questiontext.text: Why should editors verify Wikidata QIDs and VIAF IDs proposed by an AI model?

generalfeedback.text: AI models can draft Wikidata and VIAF identifiers for historical entities, but editors must confirm that each link points to the correct individual.

answer.text: Because models can confuse individuals sharing similar names, linking a historical figure to the wrong person.

feedback.text: Correct. Authority identifiers must point to the exact historical person, not an uncle or namesake.

answer.text: Because Wikidata charges a fee every time a QID is accessed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Wikidata is a free, open-access knowledge base.

answer.text: Because VIAF IDs expire after thirty days.

feedback.text: Incorrect. VIAF identifiers are permanent, persistent library authority numbers.

answer.text: Because TEI XML does not allow external web links.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI supports external authority links through attributes like @ref and @corresp.

name.text: 16 Question: Detecting Model Sycophancy and Leading Prompts

questiontext.text: What happens when an editor prompts an AI model with a leading, biased question?

generalfeedback.text: Write neutral prompts without leading assumptions to prevent AI models from generating flattering but false historical theories.

answer.text: The model exhibits sycophancy, flattering the editor by generating elaborate justifications for the false premise.

feedback.text: Correct. Language models tend to confirm user biases unless prompted neutrally.

answer.text: The model immediately disconnects from the internet in protest.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models do not have emotional protests; they generate text matching the prompt's tone.

answer.text: The model deletes all files in the editor's workspace.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Text generation queries cannot delete local project files.

answer.text: The model forces the user to retake the course quiz.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI chat interfaces do not administer university course grading policies.

name.text: 17 Question: Multi-Model Cross-Verification Pipelines

questiontext.text: In a multi-model verification pipeline, what does a disagreement between two AI models signify?

generalfeedback.text: Running prompts across two different models highlights factual disagreements and flags passages that require close human review.

answer.text: It flags a factual discrepancy, ambiguous historical evidence, or a translation difficulty requiring close human investigation.

feedback.text: Correct. Where models disagree, the human editor must examine primary sources to establish ground truth.

answer.text: It proves that both computers have suffered permanent hardware failures.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Model disagreement is a standard statistical outcome, not a hardware breakdown.

answer.text: It means the historical document must be completely discarded.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Ambiguity in historical texts is normal and requires scholarly interpretation.

answer.text: It indicates that one of the models has become sentient.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI models are pattern-matching software tools, not conscious beings.

name.text: 18 Question: The Four-Step Forensic Fact-Checking Protocol

questiontext.text: What is the first step in the four-step forensic fact-checking protocol for AI commentary?

generalfeedback.text: Follow a four-step audit protocol—checking quotations, entities, citations, and XML anchors—before accepting any AI note.

answer.text: A quotation check, confirming that every quoted string matches the primary transcription character for character.

feedback.text: Correct. Step 1 verifies that the AI did not alter, modernize, or fabricate the quoted manuscript words.

answer.text: Publishing the unvetted draft on social media.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unvetted drafts should never be published publicly.

answer.text: Translating the note into Latin and back into English.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Round-trip translation adds noise rather than verifying quotes.

answer.text: Formatting the text as a printed PDF book.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Verification must occur before final presentation typesetting.

name.text: 19 Question: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Validation Protocols

questiontext.text: Under the HITL decision framework, when should an editor choose the REVISE action for an AI draft?

generalfeedback.text: The human editor holds final authority, classifying every AI proposal as Accept, Revise, Reject, or Flag.

answer.text: When the draft provides sound historical context, but its prose contains modern clichés, wordiness, or a minor factual error.

feedback.text: Correct. REVISE salvages useful background while polishing style and correcting minor inaccuracies.

answer.text: When the draft is completely fabricated and must be thrown into the trash.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Fabricated notes should be marked REJECT, not REVISE.

answer.text: When the draft is 100% perfect and needs no changes whatsoever.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Flawless notes should be marked ACCEPT.

answer.text: When the editor does not know what the document means.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unresolved questions should be marked FLAG for further archive research.

name.text: 20 Question: The Commentary Ledger: COMMENTARY.md

questiontext.text: What is the scholarly purpose of maintaining a COMMENTARY.md ledger in your repository?

generalfeedback.text: The COMMENTARY.md ledger logs the origin, audit notes, and editorial decision for every note in your digital edition.

answer.text: To document the provenance, audit notes, and editorial decisions for every commentary note with full transparency.

feedback.text: Correct. A ledger provides an auditable record demonstrating how human expertise governed computational drafting.

answer.text: To hide computational mistakes from course instructors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The ledger explicitly documents mistakes and corrections to demonstrate critical thinking.

answer.text: To replace the need for writing a final term paper.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The ledger is a research tracking tool, not a substitute for scholarly writing.

answer.text: To store encrypted passwords for your GitHub account.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Security credentials must never be stored in markdown repository files.

name.text: 21 Question: Hands-On: Prompting for Ace's 1791 French Decree

questiontext.text: When prompting for historical commentary on the 1791 assignat decree, why specify the 5-livre denomination?

generalfeedback.text: Prompting for historical decrees requires specifying denominations, legislative context, and strict negative constraints against fake dates.

answer.text: Because 5-livre notes represented a crucial shift to small currency for paying workers and soldiers, addressing coin hoarding.

feedback.text: Correct. Denomination context explains the economic necessity of issuing small paper notes during the Revolution.

answer.text: Because 5 livres was the exact price of an iPad in 1791 Paris.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Consumer electronics did not exist in 18th-century France.

answer.text: Because King Louis XVI refused to touch paper money larger than five livres.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The King's personal preferences did not govern revolutionary monetary policy.

answer.text: Because the French language only had words for numbers up to five.

feedback.text: Incorrect. French mathematics and vocabulary possessed complete numerical systems.

name.text: 22 Question: Hands-On: Prompting for Olyvia's 1967 Maud Lewis Letter

questiontext.text: Why must prompts regarding Maud Lewis's 1967 letter include guardrails against mentioning commercial art galleries?

generalfeedback.text: Prompting for personal letters requires strict biographical guardrails to avoid confusing private correspondence with commercial gallery business.

answer.text: Because Maud Lewis sold her paintings directly from her Digby home or through personal mail, not through formal commercial galleries.

feedback.text: Correct. Guardrails prevent the model from projecting modern commercial art marketing onto a humble folk artist.

answer.text: Because commercial art galleries were strictly illegal in Nova Scotia in 1967.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commercial galleries existed in Canada, but Maud Lewis did not use them.

answer.text: Because Maud Lewis was an undercover police detective.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Maud Lewis was an internationally celebrated Canadian folk painter.

answer.text: Because the letter was written on gallery letterhead.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The letter was handwritten on plain correspondence paper.

name.text: 23 Question: Hands-On: Prompting for Andromeda's 1752 Treaty

questiontext.text: Why should a prompt for the 1752 Treaty forbid citing 21st-century court cases?

generalfeedback.text: Treaty commentary requires careful historical balancing, connecting 18th-century agreements to prior treaties while excluding modern legal anachronisms.

answer.text: To ensure the generated commentary explains the agreement within its authentic 1752 historical and diplomatic context.

feedback.text: Correct. Historical commentary explains what terms meant to the original signatories, avoiding modern legal anachronism.

answer.text: Because 21st-century court cases are secret and classified.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern court judgments are public legal records.

answer.text: Because Canadian courts have never cited the 1752 Treaty.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Canadian courts have extensively analyzed historical peace treaties.

answer.text: Because the AI model will crash if it reads modern legal citations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models process modern legal text easily; the constraint preserves historical focus.

name.text: 24 Question: Hands-On: The Hallucination Hunt (Catching Fabricated Sources)

questiontext.text: In the hallucination hunt exercise, how do we know the citation to 'Dr. Ronald MacFarlane (1984)' was fabricated?

generalfeedback.text: Practicing hallucination hunts sharpens your editorial eye to catch fake articles, phantom books, and invented historical events.

answer.text: No scholar by that name published 'Colonial Treaties of Acadia' with University of Toronto Press in 1984; the model invented the citation.

feedback.text: Correct. Verifying citations against library catalogs confirms that the book and author do not exist.

answer.text: Because books published in 1984 were printed entirely in purple ink.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 1984 books were printed using standard black ink.

answer.text: Because University of Toronto Press only publishes medical books.

feedback.text: Incorrect. University of Toronto Press is a renowned publisher of Canadian history.

answer.text: Because all treaties from Acadia were destroyed in a flood in 1800.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Treaties from the Maritime region survive in official government archives.

name.text: 25 Question: Hands-On: Vetting Tone, Grammar, and Style

questiontext.text: Why should editors eliminate clichés like 'serves as a testament to' and 'rich tapestry' from AI drafts?

generalfeedback.text: Vetting style means removing AI clichés and wordiness, producing clear and direct explanations for your readers.

answer.text: Because empty buzzwords inflate sentence length without providing specific historical evidence or clear explanation.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly commentary values direct, concise prose that explains concrete evidence without decorative filler.

answer.text: Because the words 'testament' and 'tapestry' are copyright protected by Microsoft.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Common words cannot be copyrighted by software companies.

answer.text: Because TEI XML does not permit the letter 'T' inside note elements.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI supports all standard Unicode alphabetic characters.

answer.text: Because students lose points if their notes contain fewer than 500 words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Concise commentary notes are preferred over bloated, repetitive text.

name.text: 26 Question: Hands-On: Converting Vetted AI Notes to TEI Standoff XML

questiontext.text: Where are commentary notes stored within a TEI document according to the standoff annotation model?

generalfeedback.text: Encode vetted notes into TEI standOff elements, using resp attributes to maintain transparent records of AI assistance and human editing.

answer.text: Inside the element, grouped in an and linked to the transcription via @target attributes.

feedback.text: Correct. Standoff markup keeps the primary transcription clean by isolating interpretive notes in a separate container.

answer.text: Scattered randomly between words inside tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. In-line note embedding clutters primary transcription markup.

answer.text: In a separate Microsoft Word document saved on a flash drive.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI standoff commentary is stored in the same XML file or linked XML document.

answer.text: In the computer's motherboard BIOS memory.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI markup is stored in standard text files, not motherboard hardware memory.

name.text: 27 Question: Hands-On: Serializing Vetted Commentary as W3C JSON-LD

questiontext.text: In a W3C Web Annotation JSON-LD file, what is the role of the TextQuoteSelector?

generalfeedback.text: Serializing vetted notes as W3C JSON-LD distinguishes human creator from AI generator, enabling open web annotation sharing.

answer.text: It anchors the annotation to exact words in the target document, ensuring resilience even if character offsets shift slightly.

feedback.text: Correct. TextQuoteSelector matches exact text snippets, making annotations robust against minor markup edits.

answer.text: It automatically purchases the painting mentioned in the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Web annotations describe data; they do not conduct financial purchases.

answer.text: It deletes any quotation marks found in the document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Selectors identify text spans; they do not alter source content.

answer.text: It translates the annotation into Chinese characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language translation is governed by separate processes, not quotation selectors.

name.text: 28 Question: The Three-Way Comparative Audit Matrix

questiontext.text: According to the Three-Way Comparative Audit Matrix, what is the primary strength of manual commentary authoring (Tuesday)?

generalfeedback.text: Combining manual close reading, rule-based text search, and vetted AI drafts creates a resilient and balanced commentary workflow.

answer.text: High precision and verified accuracy, guided by careful human reading and historical expertise.

feedback.text: Correct. Manual drafting ensures trustworthy scholarship, though it requires significant time and labor.

answer.text: It takes zero seconds to draft fifty notes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual authoring is slow and labor-intensive.

answer.text: It automatically checks every library in the world simultaneously.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Human memory and search capacity are limited.

answer.text: It requires no knowledge of historical grammar or context.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manual commentary depends directly on human philological and historical knowledge.

name.text: 29 Question: Ethical Transparency and Scholarly Provenance

questiontext.text: Why must a digital edition include an Editorial Method Statement disclosing AI assistance?

generalfeedback.text: Ethical scholarship requires full disclosure of AI drafting tools, documenting editorial audit procedures, and claiming final human responsibility.

answer.text: To uphold academic integrity by making research methods transparent and establishing human responsibility for final claims.

feedback.text: Correct. Transparent disclosure is essential for ethical scholarship and reproducible research.

answer.text: To allow the AI model to receive university course credit.

feedback.text: Incorrect. AI software cannot earn academic degrees or university credit.

answer.text: Because the government fines scholars who use computers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Digital scholarship is widely encouraged and supported by academic institutions.

answer.text: To prevent students from submitting their homework on time.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Method statements clarify research procedures; they do not delay submissions.

name.text: 30 Question: Synthesis: Completing the Commentary Cycle and Preparing for Assignment 12

questiontext.text: What are the three components of the 4+3+3 grading rubric for Assignment 12?

generalfeedback.text: Assignment 12 brings together manual precision, standoff TEI markup, and comparative audit reflections, due Friday, December 4 at 11:00 PM.

answer.text: Manual Ground Truth Precision (4 pts), Standoff TEI Markup Validity (3 pts), and Comparative Audit Reflection (3 pts).

feedback.text: Correct. The rubric evaluates accurate notes (40%), valid TEI standoff markup (30%), and the COMMENTARY.md ledger (30%).

answer.text: Attendance (4 pts), Typing Speed (3 pts), and Laptop Battery Life (3 pts).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Course assignments evaluate digital editing skills, not typing speed or battery life.

answer.text: Buying Coffee (4 pts), Cleaning the Lab (3 pts), and Printing Posters (3 pts).

feedback.text: Incorrect. Assignment 12 evaluates textual editing, TEI markup, and critical reflection.

answer.text: Memorizing Dates (4 pts), Drawing Maps (3 pts), and Reciting Speeches (3 pts).

feedback.text: Incorrect. The course focuses on digital scholarly editing methods.
